props.title: Midnight
props.initialSlug: Love blooms in Paris between unlikely soulmates

sections.content: Midnight (1939) stands as one of screwball comedy's most sophisticated achievements, featuring Claudette Colbert as a penniless showgirl who poses as a wealthy aristocrat in Paris. Director Mitchell Leisen, working from a razor-sharp script by Billy Wilder and Charles Brackett, crafts a perfect blend of romantic farce and social satire. The film shares DNA with other elite screwball classics like The Lady Eve (1941) and Easy Living (1937), particularly in its exploration of class mobility and mistaken identity. Colbert's chemistry with Don Ameche creates the same electric spark that defines It Happened One Night (1934).

sections.content: The film exemplifies the height of Paramount's sophisticated comedy style of the late 1930s. Like Trouble in Paradise (1932) and Design for Living (1933), it combines European sophistication with American screwball energy. The lavish Art Deco sets and Travis Banton's costumes create a glamorous backdrop for social climbing and romantic deception. John Barrymore delivers one of his final great performances as the manipulative Georges Flammarion, reminiscent of his work in Twentieth Century (1934). SUBHEAD: The Art of Screwball Sophistication

What sets Midnight apart is its perfect balance of wit and warmth. While many screwball comedies like The Awful Truth (1937) and Bringing Up Baby (1938) lean heavily into slapstick, Leisen maintains an air of sophistication even in the most farcical moments. The film's structure influenced later romantic comedies about social imposture, from Sabrina (1954) to Pretty Woman (1990).
